title: How to handle 1099-nec corrections on Mac: Type 1 or Type 2, and what each costs
metaTitle: 1099-nec corrections on Mac: Type 1 vs Type 2 fixes
description: Fix a wrong 1099-NEC on Mac. Learn when one corrected return is enough, when you need two, what IRS penalties cost, and how to file.
intro: To correct a 1099-NEC, first sort the mistake. A wrong amount, wrong box, or wrong checkbox takes one corrected return. A wrong payee name, wrong TIN, or wrong form type takes two filings: a zeroed corrected return, then a new original. The penalty clock matters too, so start this week.
tldr: Wrong amount, code, or checkbox: file one corrected return with the CORRECTED box checked.
Wrong payee name, TIN, or form type: file a zeroed corrected return first, then a new original.
IRS penalties rise with delay: $60 per return within 30 days after the due date, $340 after August 1.
Corrections go through the same channel as the original. Check how the first filing went out.
On QuickBooks Desktop for Mac, the correction path is not in the Intuit article I checked. Confirm before you file.

blocks.text: Start with the error type, not the form

Most 1099-NEC fixes go wrong at the start. People open the software before they decide what kind of mistake they made. The IRS sorts errors into two types, and each type has its own path. Type 1 covers a wrong money amount, a wrong code, a wrong checkbox, or a return filed when none was required. Type 2 covers a missing or incorrect payee TIN, an incorrect payee name, or the wrong form type. Type 1 takes one corrected return. Type 2 takes two filings.

Check the amount before you check the name, and write down the type for each row. A wrong amount with the right TIN is usually a one-return fix. A right amount with a wrong TIN is a two-step fix, even though the money looks correct. Keep this list in a spreadsheet, one row per payee and box. The list becomes your record of what you filed and why.

blocks.text: What a Type 1 correction looks like

A Type 1 correction is one new return. You file it as a corrected return and check the CORRECTED box. The corrected return shows the right numbers in the right boxes. Say a contractor was paid $4,200 for the year, but your original 1099-NEC showed $2,400 in box 1. That is a Type 1 error. You file one corrected 1099-NEC showing $4,200 with the CORRECTED box checked. Then you give the contractor a corrected copy so their records match yours.

Do not use the VOID box for this fix. The IRS says the CORRECTED box corrects a form already filed. An X in the VOID box only voids a form before you submit it. Checking VOID on a return the IRS already has fixes nothing. The wrong figure stays on file.
How a Type 2 correction works in two steps

A Type 2 correction takes two filings, and the order matters. The first is a corrected return. It repeats the original payer, recipient, and account data exactly as you filed it. Every money amount is -0-. You check the CORRECTED box. This step zeroes out the wrong record. The second is the correct return. You prepare it as an original, so you leave the CORRECTED box empty. It carries the right name, the right TIN, and the right amounts.

Here is a worked case. A $9,800 payment went out under the wrong TIN. Step one: file a corrected return with the TIN, name, and account number exactly as you filed them, and -0- in every money box. Check CORRECTED. Step two: file a new original with the right TIN, the same name, and $9,800 in box 1. Leave CORRECTED unchecked. Then send the contractor the correct statement.

blocks.title: Keep the order
blocks.text: File the zeroed corrected return before the new original. The IRS instructions list the steps in that order, so follow it. If your software offers only one correction button, check which step it creates before you press anything.
Form 1096 notation for paper filers

If you filed on paper, a Type 2 correction also needs a notation on the new Form 1096. Write one phrase in the bottom margin: Filed To Correct TIN., Filed To Correct Name., or Filed To Correct Return. Pick the phrase that matches the error. Paper filers who find any error must correct it as soon as possible. File Copy A with a new Form 1096 at the IRS Submission Processing Center. Then furnish recipient statements that show the correction.
Paper, e-file, and the same channel rule

A correction travels the way the original did. If you e-filed the original, correct it by e-file. If you filed on paper, correct it on paper. Check how the first filing went out before you start, so you do not have to guess later. Intuit's QuickBooks Online article uses the same rule. Corrections must be filed the same way as the original.

items: Original e-filed: correct it by e-file, through the same service.
Original on paper: file Copy A with a new Form 1096 at the IRS Submission Processing Center.
Original rejected by the IRS: void it and refile. Do not try to correct it.
Every contractor: give a corrected statement. QuickBooks Online does not send corrected forms for you.

blocks.text: How to correct a 1099-NEC in QuickBooks Online

Intuit's help article on correcting 1099s, updated 10/15/2026, lists the steps below. QuickBooks Online corrects only forms the IRS has accepted. Menu names can shift, so match the labels you see on your own screen. Work in your browser, and read each screen before you click.

items: Confirm the original shows Accepted. If it does not, stop and read the next step.
If the IRS rejected the original, void it and refile instead of correcting it.
Fix the contractor information first, such as the name, TIN, or address.
Review the account-to-box mapping, so each account feeds the box you expect.

blocks.text: Two changes need extra steps. A filer name or EIN change needs a letter to the IRS, because a form alone does not cover it. An address-only change needs no corrected form at all. If the corrected total falls below the reporting threshold, QuickBooks Online shows the corrected total as $0.00. Corrections for other states must be filed separately.
How to correct a 1099-NEC in QuickBooks Desktop for Mac

QuickBooks Desktop for Mac uses a different route. Intuit's article gives the 1099 path as Vendors > 1099 Forms > Print or E-file 1099/1096. From there, choose Get started on 1099-NECs. If you choose E-file, QuickBooks imports your 1099 data into a Tax1099 account. Edits you make in Tax1099 do not update the QuickBooks company file. Keep both records in step before you file.

Here is the gap. The Desktop article I checked says nothing about corrected 1099s. It also does not name a Desktop for Mac version. Older Intuit community threads say a Mac cannot e-file directly, but the current article describes the Tax1099 route. Confirm your version and your filing channel with Intuit before you correct anything. If you use QuickBooks Desktop Payroll and e-filed through Tax1099, Intuit says to make corrections in Tax1099.
What late corrections cost in IRS penalties

The penalty depends on timing, not only on the error. The IRS general instructions list per-return tiers. A return corrected within 30 days after the due date costs $60. A return filed more than 30 days late, but by August 1, costs $130. A return filed after August 1, or not filed, costs $340. Each tier has an annual maximum, and the IRS lists a lower maximum for small businesses.

Put numbers on it. Suppose 40 returns are wrong, and you correct every one within 30 days after the due date. That comes to 40 times $60, or $2,400. If the same 40 returns are not filed until after August 1, the math is 40 times $340, or $13,600. The difference is $11,200 for the same 40 mistakes. These are example results on the IRS tiers, not an estimate of your exposure.

Intentional disregard is a separate category. The IRS says it carries a penalty of at least $680 per information return, with no maximum. In plain terms, it is about ignoring a known filing problem. If you are not sure where your situation falls, ask your firm's tax lead or a licensed tax professional before you file. Do not rely on a chatbot for that call.
Why 1099-NEC errors happen

No primary study I found explains why 1099 errors happen. This section is reasoning from the rules and one audit finding. The closest number comes from the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration, reported in May 2021 for tax year 2018. It counted 182,075 payers who filed 440,404 information returns with a missing or incorrect payee TIN. I read that finding through Accounting Today, not the TIGTA report itself. It concerns backup withholding, not corrections.
The causes listed below are points where the rules are easy to break. Check them first when you build your list.
A mixed batch, worked through

Say you filed 12 returns in January. Three need fixing. These examples are invented for practice. Contractor A has $1,000 typed as $100 in box 1. That is Type 1, so one corrected 1099-NEC with the CORRECTED box checked fixes it. Contractor B has a TIN one digit off. That is Type 2, so one zeroed corrected return, then one new original. Contractor C was paid for rent, so the form should have been a 1099-MISC. That is also Type 2. You file a zeroed corrected 1099-NEC, then a new original 1099-MISC.

Count the filings. Contractor A needs one. Contractors B and C each need two, so the batch needs five filings in total. Write the decision next to each row before you open any software. If your list lives in Excel, press ⌘ F to find each payee fast. For more on working with accountant spreadsheets, see [Excel for accountants on Mac](/for/accountants/excel).
Mistakes that create a second correction

items: Checking VOID on a form the IRS already has.
Filing the new original before the zeroed corrected return.
Leaving CORRECTED checked on the new original in a Type 2 fix.
Correcting a rejected form instead of voiding and refiling it.
Editing a 1099 in Tax1099 and assuming the QuickBooks company file changed too.
Forgetting to give the contractor a corrected statement.

blocks.text: Each of these creates a second round of work. Before you file, read the form header and each changed box against your row. Then read it once more against the W-9 on file.
Check the current IRS instructions before you file

This page explains the mechanics. It is not your filing instructions. The IRS guide I used lists the 1099-NEC reporting amount as $600 or more, with January 31 as the due date. One IRS page I read gave February 2 for 2026, so the due date is unresolved in my notes. The penalty tiers come from the 2025 instructions page, and I did not verify the 2026 caps. Open the current general instructions yourself before you rely on any amount.

If you prepare forms for a client or employer, follow their rules on taxpayer data. Full TINs and payee names are sensitive. Do not paste them into a chat tool, a shared document, or an email unless your firm allows it. Lazur listens and looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. Its privacy notes say audio and screenshots go to AI providers to answer and are not stored. Your firm's rules still come first.
Where Lazur fits, and where it does not

Lazur helps with the reading and the walk-through. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where a menu is, and Lazur circles it and labels it. Ask how to do something, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click. Lazur does not click buttons or operate other apps for you. You still file in the software, under your own login.
What to do next

Start with one list. Sort every flagged return into Type 1 or Type 2, and note the penalty tier each one would face if it slips past a deadline. Fix the Type 1 rows first, because each needs one filing. Then work the Type 2 rows in order, zeroed return first. Give each contractor a corrected statement, and keep a copy of every filing with your records.

faq.question: Can I correct a 1099-NEC by filing a fresh copy?
faq.answer: Not by itself. The IRS instructions describe corrections with the CORRECTED box. For a Type 1 error, check CORRECTED on the corrected return. For a Type 2 error, file a zeroed corrected return first, then a new original without the box.

faq.question: What is the difference between CORRECTED and VOID?
faq.answer: CORRECTED fixes a form already filed with the IRS. VOID only voids a form before you submit it. An X in the VOID box does not correct a return that already went in.

faq.question: Does the contractor need a corrected copy too?
faq.answer: Yes, in practice. For paper filers, the IRS says to furnish recipient statements that show the correction. QuickBooks Online does not send corrected forms to the contractor, so you send them yourself.

faq.question: What if QuickBooks Online says the original was rejected?
faq.answer: Void it and refile. Intuit says corrections are possible only after the IRS accepts the original. Rejected forms must be voided and refiled instead.

faq.question: Do I need a corrected form for a new address?
faq.answer: No. Intuit's article says an address-only change needs no corrected form. Update your records so the next filing season starts clean.

faq.question: What if the business name or EIN changed?
faq.answer: That needs a letter to the IRS. Intuit's article says a filer name or EIN change requires a letter, so a corrected form alone does not cover it.

faq.question: How much is the penalty for a late correction?
faq.answer: The 2025 IRS instructions list $60 per return within 30 days after the due date, $130 for filings more than 30 days late but by August 1, and $340 after August 1 or if never filed. Intentional disregard carries at least $680 per return. Confirm these amounts for your filing year.

faq.question: Can I fix a 1099-NEC in QuickBooks Desktop for Mac?
faq.answer: Intuit's Desktop article gives the path to 1099 forms and mentions Tax1099 for e-file. It does not cover corrected 1099s. Confirm the correction route with Intuit before you file.

faq.question: Can Lazur file the correction for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons, edit files, or operate other apps for you. It answers out loud, points at things, and guides you one click at a time. You file in your own software.

faq.question: Can I paste a TIN into an AI tool to check it?
faq.answer: Follow your employer's or client's rules on taxpayer data first. If your firm does not allow it, check the record yourself against the W-9 and your software, and keep the data out of chat tools.

costs.title: Penalties add up per return
costs.text: The IRS counts penalties per return, so a small batch can get expensive. Under the 2025 tiers, a return corrected within 30 days after the due date costs $60. A return filed after August 1, or never filed, costs $340. The tier depends on timing, so waiting is the cost you control most.

costs.title: Hours spent on the second filing
costs.text: Type 2 errors cost more time than Type 1 errors because they need two filings. Paper filings also need the Form 1096 notation. I did not find a published number for how long these fixes take. Track your own minutes on the next batch. That log tells you more than a guess.

costs.title: A contractor who gets the wrong record
costs.text: A contractor who receives a wrong statement has to ask you or fix their own records. A corrected statement avoids that back and forth. Send it, and keep proof that you sent it.

costs.title: Backup withholding risk from bad TINs
costs.text: A missing or incorrect TIN has a cost beyond the form. The TIGTA finding, as reported by Accounting Today, says $13.3 billion was not backup withheld on $55.6 billion of reported income in tax year 2018. That is a system-wide figure, not your exposure. It shows why the TIN check belongs in your routine.

causes.title: TIN typed wrong or never collected
causes.text: A TIN that was never collected, or was typed with a transposed digit, is a Type 2 error. The only cause-level evidence I found points at missing or incorrect TINs. The TIGTA finding covers 440,404 information returns in tax year 2018. Collect the W-9 before the first payment, and check the TIN against it when you enter the payee.

causes.title: Legal name differs from the name you entered
causes.text: A business can have a legal name, a trade name, and an owner's name. If the form uses one name and the IRS record uses another, the name fails to match. The fix is a Type 2 correction. Use the exact legal name from the W-9, not the name in the invoice header.

causes.title: Wrong form type for the payment
causes.text: If a payment belongs on a 1099-MISC, filing it as a 1099-NEC is a wrong form type. That error also needs the two-step fix. Check the payment category before you file, not after. Sort by category in your spreadsheet to spot mismatches fast.

causes.title: Account mapped to the wrong box
causes.text: Accounting software maps each expense account to a 1099 box. A mapping that points at the wrong box can produce wrong amounts for every payee tied to it. QuickBooks Online asks you to review account-to-box mapping during a correction, so the mapping is worth checking first. This cause is reasoning from the workflow, not a measured rate.

causes.title: Late or split payments in the wrong year
causes.text: A bill paid late, or a payment split across two accounts, can land in the wrong total. When only the amount is wrong, that is a Type 1 error. Check the payment dates against the calendar year on the form before you trust a total.

fixes.title: Sort every error into Type 1 or Type 2 first
fixes.text: Use the table in this guide and write one decision per row. Do not start in the software. A Type 1 row and a Type 2 row need different filings. Mixing them up creates the second correction you wanted to avoid. Keep the list as your record.

fixes.title: Fix Type 1 with one corrected return
fixes.text: File one corrected return with the CORRECTED box checked. Show the right amount, code, or checkbox. Use the same channel as the original. Do not use VOID for a form the IRS already has. Then give the contractor a corrected copy.

fixes.title: Fix Type 2 with a zeroed return, then a new original
fixes.text: File the zeroed corrected return first. Repeat the original payer, recipient, and account data, with -0- in every money box. Then file the correct return as an original, with the CORRECTED box empty. On paper, add the Form 1096 notation: Filed To Correct TIN., Filed To Correct Name., or Filed To Correct Return.

fixes.title: Void and refile a rejected form
fixes.text: A rejected form has no accepted record to correct. Intuit says to void the rejected form and refile it. Confirm the original status before you choose a path. If you skip that check, you can end up trying to correct something the IRS never accepted.

fixes.title: Handle name, EIN, and address changes separately
fixes.text: A change to the filer name or EIN needs a letter to the IRS. An address-only change needs no corrected form, according to Intuit's QuickBooks Online article. Sort these out before you file any corrected return, so you do not file a form you did not need.

fixes.title: Match each record to the W-9 on file
fixes.text: Open the W-9 for each payee. Compare the legal name and TIN against the record in your software. In Excel or Numbers, copy those two columns into one sheet and flag any mismatch. In Excel, ⌘ F helps you find a specific name fast. Use only the fields your firm allows.

fixes.title: Correct the software record too
fixes.text: Fixing the IRS filing does not fix your books by itself. In QuickBooks Desktop, edits made in Tax1099 do not update the company file. After each correction, check that the record in your books matches what you filed. That keeps next year's list clean.

fixes.title: Keep a correction log
fixes.text: Write one line per correction: payee, box, error type, filing date, acceptance status, and the date you sent the contractor a corrected statement. A plain spreadsheet works. If you dictate notes on a Mac, hold fn to dictate text at the cursor in any app, then check it before you save.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Build the list
plan.text: Pull every 1099-NEC you filed this year. Mark each row as correct, Type 1, or Type 2. Keep the list in Excel or Numbers, with one row per payee and box.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Check names and TINs
plan.text: Compare each legal name and TIN with the W-9 on file. Flag every mismatch. Do not paste full TINs into shared or AI tools unless your firm allows it.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: File the Type 1 fixes
plan.text: File each Type 1 correction as one corrected return with the CORRECTED box checked. Confirm the acceptance status in your filing channel before you move on.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Work the Type 2 rows
plan.text: For each Type 2 row, file the zeroed corrected return first, then the new original. On paper, add the Form 1096 notation that matches the error.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Notify and log
plan.text: Send each contractor a corrected statement and log the date and method. Add a reminder in Apple Reminders to rerun the W-9 check before the next filing season.
